options: Motor root of the trigeminal nerve
mu-048c8f03.explanation: Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve; it presses the cheek against the teeth to stop food escaping into the vestibule. The buccal nerve (V3) is purely sensory and supplies the skin and mucosa of the cheek; the similar names are often confused.
notes: It carries sensation from the skin and mucosa of the cheek; it does not supply the muscle.
It supplies the muscles of mastication.

mu-088bce2a.stem: A patient with an ischaemic stroke in the left hemisphere has a drooping right corner of the mouth and a flattened right nasolabial fold, but can wrinkle the forehead on both sides and close both eyes. What explains this finding?
options: The lesion is where the facial nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen.
Occipitofrontalis is supplied by cervical nerves.
The part of the facial nucleus supplying the upper face receives bilateral cortical fibres.
The lesion is in the course of the facial nerve within the pons.
The forehead muscles are supplied by the trigeminal nerve.
mu-088bce2a.explanation: In central (upper motor neuron) facial palsy only the lower half of the opposite face is affected, because the part of the facial nucleus controlling the forehead and orbicularis oculi receives corticobulbar fibres from both hemispheres. In peripheral (Bell's) palsy the whole face on the same side is involved.

mu-efaaeac6.stem: A patient with Bell's palsy cannot close the right eye and complains of a dry eye. Which muscle closes the eye, and what is its nerve?
mu-efaaeac6.explanation: Orbicularis oculi, which closes the eyelids, is supplied by the temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve. When it is paralysed the eye cannot close, the cornea dries and the efferent limb of the corneal reflex is lost. Levator, which raises the lid, is supplied by the oculomotor nerve.

mu-09e47eb9.stem: Which muscle of mastication opens the mouth (protrudes and depresses the mandible)?
mu-09e47eb9.explanation: Three of the four muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) close the jaw. Lateral pterygoid initiates opening by pulling the condyle and disc forwards; gravity and the suprahyoid muscles complete the movement. All the muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).

mu-a970e178.stem: Which is the main muscle that retracts the mandible?
mu-a970e178.explanation: The fan-shaped fibres of temporalis run to the coronoid process. The anterior and middle fibres close the jaw; the almost horizontal posterior fibres pull the mandible backwards.

mu-f3f3e968.stem: After a head injury a patient reports double vision, especially when going downstairs and reading; he holds his head tilted to the healthy side. Which muscle is paralysed?
mu-f3f3e968.explanation: Superior oblique (trochlear nerve, IV) turns the eye down, especially when adducted, and intorts it. When paralysed there is vertical diplopia on looking down and in (going downstairs, reading); the patient tilts the head to the opposite side to compensate for the extorsion. The trochlear nerve is often injured in head trauma because of its long intracranial course.

mu-449f4db6.stem: In abducens nerve palsy, what is the resting position of the affected eye?
mu-449f4db6.explanation: The abducens nerve (VI) supplies only lateral rectus. In its palsy the unopposed medial rectus pulls the eye inwards (esotropia) and there is horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze. The 'down and out' position is characteristic of oculomotor palsy.

mu-1758e4b6.stem: Which nerve supplies levator palpebrae superioris?
mu-1758e4b6.explanation: Levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve; in III palsy there is complete ptosis. Its smooth muscle part, the superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle, is supplied by sympathetic fibres; the mild ptosis of Horner syndrome is due to this.

mu-54efdbc4.stem: When the patient protrudes the tongue it deviates to the right. Which nerve and side is the lesion on?
mu-54efdbc4.explanation: Genioglossus, which protrudes the tongue, pushes it forwards and towards the opposite side from each side. In a unilateral XII palsy the healthy side dominates and the tongue deviates towards the paralysed side (the side of the lesion). In chronic lesions there is wasting and fasciculation on that side.

mu-a9ba69fb.stem: Which of the following tongue muscles is NOT supplied by the hypoglossal nerve?
mu-a9ba69fb.explanation: All intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve; the only exception is palatoglossus, regarded as a muscle of the soft palate, which receives a branch of the vagus (pharyngeal plexus).

mu-b6febbff.stem: Which muscle wrinkles the forehead and raises the eyebrows?
mu-b6febbff.explanation: The frontal belly of occipitofrontalis pulls the galea aponeurotica forwards, raises the eyebrows and forms horizontal lines on the forehead. The frontal belly is supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve, the occipital belly by the posterior auricular nerve.

mu-e85000e2.stem: Which muscle draws the corner of the mouth upwards and outwards when smiling?
mu-e85000e2.explanation: Zygomaticus major arises from the zygomatic bone and attaches to the modiolus at the corner of the mouth, producing the smiling expression. Depressor anguli oris pulls the corner of the mouth down, giving a sad expression.

mu-171212d9.stem: Which muscle, contracting on one side, tilts the head towards the same shoulder and turns the face to the opposite side and upwards?
mu-171212d9.explanation: SCM runs from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process. Contracting on one side it tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side; on both sides it flexes the head. In congenital torticollis the muscle becomes fibrosed and shortened. Its motor nerve is the accessory nerve.
